lead: Avionics electronics is the layer between a transducer and a computer. A pressure sensor gives a few millivolts; an ADC needs volts and a clean signal. Diodes protect, transistors switch and amplify, op-amps condition, ADCs digitise, DACs drive actuators, and a microcontroller runs the loop. The same chain appears in an air-data computer, a fuel-quantity unit or a flap controller. This chapter follows one signal from bridge to actuator and gives the numbers an exam asks for.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.10 on transducers and basic electronics (voltage, current, resistance).

sections.h3: Diodes and transistors: protection and control

blocks.text: A diode is a two-terminal one-way valve. Current flows from anode to cathode when the anode is about 0.7 V higher for silicon. Reverse bias blocks current until breakdown. In avionics a diode does three jobs. A rectifier turns AC into DC in a transformer rectifier unit. A flyback diode sits across a relay or solenoid coil; when coil current stops, the stored energy circulates through the diode instead of punching a voltage spike into the transistor. A clamping diode limits an input to the supply rails.

A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has base, collector and emitter. In the active region it amplifies: a small base current controls a larger collector current. The DC current gain is β = I<sub>C</sub> / I<sub>B</sub>, where I<sub>C</sub> is collector current in amperes and I<sub>B</sub> is base current in amperes. As a switch, the BJT is driven into saturation so V<sub>CE</sub> is small and power loss is low. A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch with gate, drain and source; it carries the high current of a fuel pump, landing-light relay or flap motor, and the microcontroller drives its gate through a resistor.

items: A silicon diode drop of 0.7 V is a loss in low-voltage circuits.
A relay coil needs a flyback diode; without it the transistor sees a large inductive kick.
A MOSFET gate needs a defined pull-down so it does not switch on when the microcontroller resets.

blocks.text: An operational amplifier (op-amp) is a high-gain differential amplifier. Ideal rules: no current enters the input terminals, and the op-amp drives its output so the two input voltages are equal when negative feedback is present. These two rules solve most circuits.

Inverting amplifier: input through R<sub>in</sub> to the '-' input, feedback R<sub>f</sub> from output to '-', '+' grounded. Gain A = -R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>. Non-inverting: input to '+', feedback divider R<sub>f</sub> from output to '-', R<sub>in</sub> from '-' to ground. Gain A = 1 + R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>. A buffer is the non-inverting circuit with R<sub>f</sub> replaced by a wire (R<sub>f</sub> = 0) and R<sub>in</sub> removed, so A = 1 + 0 = 1; it gives a high input impedance and a low output impedance.
A = -R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>   and   A = 1 + R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>
blocks.where: A is voltage gain (no unit); R<sub>f</sub> is feedback resistance in ohms; R<sub>in</sub> is input resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: A bridge sensor (strain gauge, pressure capsule) gives a differential voltage of a few millivolts on top of a common-mode voltage. A differential amplifier amplifies the difference and rejects the common part. The circuit has two input resistors R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> and two feedback resistors R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>4</sub>, with R<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>3</sub> = R<sub>in</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> = R<sub>4</sub> = R<sub>f</sub>; then gain = R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>. All four equal is the special case gain = 1. In practice a resistor mismatch reduces common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR). An instrumentation amplifier uses three op-amps to give high input impedance and a set gain.

Signal conditioning means making a sensor signal fit for the ADC. Amplification raises millivolts to volts. Filtering removes 50 Hz mains pickup, vibration noise and aliasing before sampling. Isolation (optocoupler or transformer) stops a ground loop or a high common-mode voltage from damaging the computer. Linearisation corrects a thermocouple or pressure sensor curve with a polynomial or lookup table.

An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) turns a voltage into a code. For an N-bit ADC with reference V<sub>ref</sub>, the resolution (smallest step) is Q = V<sub>ref</sub> / 2<sup>N</sup>, where Q is in volts, V<sub>ref</sub> is the full-scale reference in volts and N is the number of bits. The output code is floor(V<sub>in</sub> / Q), where V<sub>in</sub> is the input voltage in volts. The code saturates at 2<sup>N</sup> − 1; inputs at or above V<sub>ref</sub> clip to full scale. With this floor rule the quantisation error is between 0 and −Q, that is, up to one step low. If the converter rounds to the nearest step, the error is up to ±Q/2. State which convention a question uses. Sampling must be at least twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist); an anti-alias filter before the ADC enforces this.
Q = V<sub>ref</sub> / 2<sup>N</sup>   and   code = floor(V<sub>in</sub> / Q)
blocks.where: Q is resolution in volts; V<sub>ref</sub> is reference voltage in volts; N is ADC bits; V<sub>in</sub> is input voltage in volts; floor rounds down to an integer code.

blocks.text: A digital-to-analog converter (DAC) does the reverse: code k gives V<sub>out</sub> = k Q. It drives a valve, a servo amplifier or a lamp dimmer. The DAC output needs a buffer to supply current; a bare DAC pin cannot drive a solenoid.

A microcontroller is a single chip with a CPU, flash program memory, RAM, digital input/output pins, timers and serial ports (UART, SPI, I²C, CAN; see Chapter 4.7). In avionics it runs a periodic loop: read the ADC, filter and scale the value, compare with a limit, update outputs, send a status word on the bus. Timers generate the sample clock and pulse-width modulation (PWM) for actuator drive. Watchdog timers reset the chip if the loop hangs. The chain is: sensor → bridge → amplifier → filter → ADC → microcontroller → DAC → actuator.

examples.question: An 8-bit ADC has a reference voltage of 5.000 V. (a) Find the resolution in volts and millivolts. (b) Find the output code for an input of 1.000 V.
steps: N = 8 bits, V<sub>ref</sub> = 5.000 V. Number of codes = 2<sup>8</sup> = 256.
Code = floor(V<sub>in</sub> / Q) = floor(1.000 V / 0.01953125 V) = floor(51.2) = 51.
Check: code 51 represents 51 × 0.01953125 V = 0.99609375 V, below 1.000 V; code 52 gives 1.015625 V, above. So 51 is correct.
examples.answer: Resolution is 0.01953125 V (19.53 mV) and the code for 1.000 V is 51.
examples.check:
Vref = 5.0
N = 8
Q = Vref / (2 ** N)
code = int(1.000 // Q)
print(Q)
print(code)

traps: An 8-bit ADC has 256 codes but 255 steps between them. For an ideal binary ADC with code 0 at 0 V, use Q = V<sub>ref</sub> / 2<sup>N</sup>, not V<sub>ref</sub> / 255.
Inverting op-amp gain has a minus sign; non-inverting gain has a plus one. Writing A = R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>in</sub> for the non-inverting circuit is a common slip.
A flyback diode must be reverse-biased in normal operation: cathode to the positive supply. Reversing it shorts the supply when the coil is energised.
A BJT used as a switch must be driven into saturation. A small base current leaves it in the active region, where it dissipates heat and may fail.
A differential amplifier rejects common-mode voltage only as well as its resistor matching allows. Gain formulas ignore CMRR; exam questions often add a common-mode term.

quiz.q: What is the function of a flyback diode across a relay coil?
quiz.a: It gives the coil current a path when the driving transistor turns off, so the inductive voltage spike is clamped and the transistor is protected.

quiz.q: Why is a buffer op-amp used between a sensor bridge and an ADC?
quiz.a: A buffer has very high input impedance, so it does not load the bridge, and low output impedance, so it can drive the ADC input and any filter without loss.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has V<sub>ref</sub> = 4.096 V. Find its resolution and the code for V<sub>in</sub> = 1.000 V.
A non-inverting op-amp has R<sub>f</sub> = 9 kΩ and R<sub>in</sub> = 1 kΩ. Find the gain and the output for a 0.2 V input. If R<sub>f</sub> drifts to 10 kΩ, what changes?
quiz.a: Gain A = 1 + 9/1 = 10. Output = 10 × 0.2 V = 2.0 V. With R<sub>f</sub> = 10 kΩ, A = 1 + 10/1 = 11, so output = 11 × 0.2 V = 2.2 V. The gain error is 10%.

quiz.q: Name four blocks inside a microcontroller.
quiz.a: CPU, program memory (flash), RAM, digital input/output pins, timers and serial ports; any four.

quiz.q: Why must an anti-alias filter precede an ADC?
quiz.a: Sampling at frequency f<sub>s</sub> cannot represent signals above f<sub>s</sub>/2. Higher frequencies fold back as false low frequencies. The anti-alias filter removes them before sampling.

quiz.q: A 12-bit ADC has V<sub>ref</sub> = 3.3 V. It reads code 2048. What input voltage does this represent?

beyond: Not for the exam. Radar and flight-control computers use radiation-hard or radiation-tolerant processes, and FPGAs implement many high-speed ADC interfaces. Slow, high-resolution pressure and temperature channels often use sigma-delta ADCs with 24-bit outputs. DO-254 is the hardware assurance counterpart to DO-178B for complex electronic hardware. Search for sigma-delta ADC, instrumentation amplifier CMRR, MOSFET gate driver and DO-254.
